opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so these are useful examples because they're the closest thing we have to a natural experiment on what happens when a state doesn't need its population to generate wealth. In most countries, the government's revenue comes from taxing people's labor and the businesses they work for. That creates a dependency: the state has to keep people healthy, educated, and reasonably happy, because they're the source of its power. In rentier states, where the wealth comes out of the ground, that dependency is much weaker.

Saudi Arabia is the cautionary version. The oil revenue flows to the state more or less regardless of what citizens do, so the government doesn't have to bargain with them in the same way. Citizens get a generous deal in material terms, with subsidies, public sector jobs, and no income tax, but they don't get much political voice. The social contract is roughly "we'll take care of you, and you won't ask for a say." That's the resource curse in political form: when rulers don't need you, your leverage over them evaporates, even if they're currently treating you well.

Norway is the hopeful counterexample. It also has enormous oil wealth, but it already had strong democratic institutions, high trust, and a culture of accountability before the money arrived. So it put the revenue into a sovereign wealth fund, set rules about how much can be spent, and kept the government answerable to voters. It shows that a state with income independent of its citizens can stay accountable if the institutions are robust enough beforehand.

The reason I find this relevant to AI is that advanced AI could turn every country into something like a rentier state. If AI systems do most of the economically valuable work, governments' revenue and power stop depending on human labor. The question becomes: do we end up more like Norway or more like Saudi Arabia? And I'm worried that even the Norway case is less reassuring than it looks. Norway still depends heavily on its citizens: they run the government, staff the military, and do most of the work outside the oil sector. Oil is a big chunk of the economy, but it isn't everything. With AI, you could have a situation where humans aren't needed for almost anything, including administration and security. That's a much more extreme decoupling than any petrostate has experienced.

So I see these as lower bounds on the problem. They tell us that removing the economic dependence on citizens tends to erode their bargaining power unless there are strong countervailing institutions, and that even good institutions were built in a world where humans remained indispensable in many other ways. We shouldn't assume our current democratic norms will hold automatically once that indispensability goes away.

r001.rationale: The response says Saudi citizens receive public-sector jobs and have little political voice, but it does not identify fear of losing those jobs or other government sinecures as a constraint on dissent.

r002.rationale: The response links Norway’s democratic institutions to accountability and rules on spending oil revenue, but does not clearly say they enabled a commitment to redistribute that wealth.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the reason I bring up those two is that they're kind of a natural experiment. The worry I have about advanced AI is that we end up in a world where governments and the economy as a whole just don't need people anymore. Historically, the reason states ended up caring about their citizens at all, I'd argue, is that they needed them. They needed people to work in the factories, to pay taxes, to fight in the army. And so even fairly self-interested rulers had an incentive to keep people educated, healthy, somewhat happy, because that's where their power came from.

And then the question is: what happens when that incentive goes away? And we actually have examples of that already, which are the rentier states, where a huge fraction of government revenue comes from something that just sits in the ground. Oil, mostly. Saudi Arabia and Norway are both in that situation, and they've gone in pretty different directions.

Saudi Arabia is, I think, closer to the worrying case. The government gets most of its money from oil, so it doesn't really depend on taxing a productive population. And what you see is a state that can basically buy off its citizens. There's a big welfare apparatus, lots of government jobs that aren't necessarily doing much, and in exchange there's not a lot of political voice. The deal is sort of: we'll take care of you, you don't get a say. And that's stable because the people don't have leverage. They can't threaten to withhold their labour in any way that matters to the regime.

Norway is the hopeful case. They also have enormous oil wealth, but they had strong democratic institutions and norms in place before the oil showed up. And they made this deliberate choice to put it in a sovereign wealth fund, with rules about how much can be spent each year, and to treat it as belonging to the population rather than to whoever's in power. So the wealth gets channelled through institutions that were already accountable, and that accountability kind of persisted even though the underlying economic reason for it had weakened.

So the lesson I take from that is: the outcome isn't determined by the economics alone. It depends a lot on what institutions you have at the moment the transition happens, and whether people are paying attention to locking in the right arrangements before their bargaining power disappears. With AI the scary part is that this could happen to basically every country at once, and most countries look more like Saudi Arabia in terms of institutional preparedness than like Norway. And Norway is kind of a lucky case even then. So I think of them as, you know, a preview of the two attractor states, and a reminder that the window to choose between them might be pretty short.

r001.rationale: The response says Saudi Arabia provides government jobs and welfare in exchange for little political voice, but it does not identify fear of losing those benefits or jobs as a constraint on dissent.

r002.rationale: The response links Norway’s preexisting strong democratic institutions to its choice to put oil wealth in a regulated sovereign wealth fund and channel it through accountable institutions.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re useful examples because a lot of the government’s revenue comes from oil, rather than from taxing people’s work. That changes the relationship between the state and its citizens. If a government needs people to be productive and pay taxes, it has a practical reason to invest in them and listen to their demands. If its income comes from something else, that particular incentive is weaker.

Saudi Arabia illustrates the concern: a state can distribute some of that wealth while giving citizens relatively little political power. Norway shows that this isn’t inevitable. You can have resource wealth alongside democracy, accountability, and broad public benefit. The institutions matter enormously.

The analogy to AI is that governments might eventually get much of their revenue from AI production without needing their citizens’ labour. That could be wonderful materially, but it could also remove an important source of ordinary people’s bargaining power. So the question is how we preserve their political power when their economic contribution is no longer something the state depends on.

r001.rationale: The response says Saudi Arabia distributes wealth while citizens have relatively little political power, but does not identify the risk of losing government sinecures as a constraint on beneficiaries’ dissent.

r002.rationale: The response associates Norway’s resource wealth with democracy and broad public benefit, but does not say strong democratic government enables a commitment to redistribute oil wealth over the short and medium term.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re useful examples because, in both cases, the state has a large source of income that doesn’t come from taxing people’s labour. And that’s potentially relevant to a world where AI does most of the economically valuable work: governments might own some of that capital, or tax it, and no longer depend very much on their citizens being productive.

That could be a very good thing. You could have a generous welfare state, and people could have much more freedom over how they spend their lives. Norway gives you some sense of what that could look like. But Saudi Arabia suggests that having enough money to support your citizens doesn’t, by itself, give them political power.

The concern is that governments currently have a practical reason to care about people: they need them to work, pay taxes, and keep the economy going. If that dependence goes away, some of the bargaining power that ordinary people have could go away with it. That doesn’t mean an oil-funded state inevitably becomes authoritarian—Norway is an obvious counterexample. It means the institutions governing that wealth matter enormously. Who owns it, who controls how it’s spent, and can citizens actually hold those people accountable?

r001.rationale: The response says Saudi Arabia suggests wealth alone does not give citizens political power, but it does not identify the risk of losing government sinecures as a constraint on beneficiaries’ political dissent.

r002.rationale: The response calls Norway an obvious counterexample and emphasizes the importance of institutions, but does not attribute Norway’s ability to redistribute oil wealth to its strong democratic government.
